title: Variables
description: How to store a value under a name so your program can use it again later.

content.text: So far you wrote every value straight into `cout`. A variable stores a value under a name. Write the name later and C++ hands you back what is inside.

parts.label: type
parts.note: The kind of value the box holds. `int` means a whole number. The type always comes first.

parts.label: name
parts.note: The label you choose. You use it later to get the value back.

parts.label: assign
parts.note: Puts the value on the right into the box named on the left.

parts.label: end
parts.note: Every C++ statement ends with a semicolon.

content.title: Anatomy of a variable
content.caption: Read it left to right: make a box for a whole number, call it `score`, put 100 in it.
No quotes means the value in the box. Quotes mean the exact characters you typed.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: The quotes make `"score"` plain text, so C++ prints the word itself. Without quotes it would open the box and print 100.

items.sub: The type is written here, once.
After declaring, use the name alone.

items.text: Or do both on one line: `int coins = 0;`
You cannot declare the same name twice.
items.sub: A second `int lives = 3;` is an error.

content.title: What C++ is holding now
content.caption: Two `int` boxes. C++ already knows their type, so later lines just use the names.

content.value: Here C++ differs from many languages. A box declared without a value is not empty and not zero. It is **uninitialised**: it holds leftover junk from that memory.

items.title: Uninitialised
items.text: Could print anything, and something different every run.

items.title: Starts known
items.text: Costs nothing and removes a whole family of strange bugs.

content.title: Junk vs a known value
content.caption: Make it a habit: give every variable a value on the line you declare it, even if it is just 0.

content.question: What does `coins` hold right after `int coins;`?
content.explain: Without a starting value, C++ leaves whatever was already in that memory. That is why you always give one.

content.value: A variable can get a new value as often as you like. The new value **replaces** the old one. The label stays, the contents change.

steps.note: Declare an `int` box named `lives` and put 3 in it.
Open the box and print what is inside.
Put 2 in the box. The 3 is gone. No type this time: the box already exists.
Print again. Same name, new value.
Right side first: `lives - 1` is 1. Then store that 1 back in `lives`.

content.title: Watch the box change
content.outro: `=` is not the equals of maths. It means: work this out, then store it here. Module 3 shows a shorthand, `lives--`, the same `++`/`--` idea as in the name C++.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: C++ works out `x + 3` first, which is 8, then stores 8 back in `x`.

items.title: Valid
items.text: Letters, digits and `_`. Do not start with a digit.

items.title: Error
items.text: Starts with a digit. Has a space. `return` is a **keyword**: a word C++ already uses.

items: C++ is case sensitive: `score` and `Score` are two different boxes.
This course uses **camelCase**: `playerScore`. Some projects use snake_case: `player_score`. Pick one and stick to it.
Pick names that say what they mean: `daysLeft`, not `d`.
content.title: Good habits

content.question: Which one is a valid C++ variable name?
content.explain: `livesLeft` uses only letters. The others start with a digit, contain a space, or are a keyword.

practice.question: Declare an `int` called `age`, store your age in it, and print it with a label, like: Age: 12
Declare `int coins = 10;`, print it, then add 5 to it using `coins = coins + 5;` and print it again.
Fix the two naming mistakes in this program so it compiles.

quiz.question: What are the three parts of `int score = 100;`?
options: A function, a name, and an instruction.
A type, a name, and a value.
quiz.explain: `int` is the type (what kind of value), `score` is the name, and `100` is the value being stored.

quiz.question: What does `cout << score << endl;` print when `score` holds 100?
quiz.explain: Without quotes, C++ looks up what is stored under that name. With quotes it would print the word score instead.

quiz.question: Which of these is a legal C++ variable name?
quiz.explain: Names cannot contain spaces or start with a digit. `highScore` also follows the camelCase style this course uses.

quiz.question: What does `lives = lives - 1;` do when `lives` holds 3?
options: Nothing: it is not a true statement.
quiz.explain: The right hand side is worked out first, giving 2, and that answer is then stored back under the same name.

quiz.question: You write `int total;` and print `total` straight away. What does it print?
options: Anything: an uninitialised variable holds leftover junk.
quiz.explain: C++ does not clear the box for you. Give every variable a starting value, such as `int total = 0;`, and the problem never appears.
